argument: Having settled on government's structure, the episode asks what government's job actually is -- Rousseau says to serve the 'general will' -- and shows how difficult that concept is to pin down and act on, since personal, group, and abstract notions of will can conflict with each other. Even once a society agrees on a shared goal, enormous disagreement remains over the path to get there and how exactly to execute it, and real-world elections often select leaders based on factors with little connection to who could best serve that goal.
keyIdeas: The three philosophers gave three different answers to what government's job is: Hobbes said maintain order, Locke said protect natural rights of life, liberty, and property, and Rousseau said serve the general will of the people.
Left unchecked, a person's personal will can lead them to expect things from government that serve only themselves and could actively harm others, rather than serving the common good.
Even a neutral-seeming law like private property protection can never be perfectly equal, since it inherently benefits people who already have more property.

Commentators split the general will into the 'democratic' version (what an assembly of citizens actually decides through debate) and the 'transcendental' version (an abstract sense of what's truly best for the common good, independent of any actual vote).

Agreeing on the general will is only step one -- governments still face enormous uncertainty over the path to achieve it and how to execute that path, as the road-trip and Iraq War examples illustrate, and real elections often select leaders on the basis of factors like ad spending or shared ethnicity rather than merit.

terms.def: Rousseau's term for what government ought to serve -- the common good, distinct from any individual's personal will.
An individual's self-interested wants, which Rousseau warns can be mistaken for what government should provide.
The general will understood as whatever citizens arrive at through assembly and debate.
The general will understood as an abstract 'best for the common good,' independent of what any actual assembly decides.
Someone who attaches their political identity to one cause, which the episode treats as a distortion of the general will.
